MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le.explanation: Pointwise, $g((x-P)/\delta)=\mathbf 1_{P<x}$ where $|P-x|>\delta$, and the two differ by at most $1$ elsewhere.

MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: as $\delta\to0^+$ the smoothed CDF converges to the CDF, $C_\delta(x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$, when $P$ has no atom at $x$
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "Pointwise values of the CDF … correspond to expected values of an indicator function, $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases." 

With the hypotheses of `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le`, let $x\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(P=x)=0$. Then $\mathrm{smoothCDF}(\mathbb P,P,g,\delta,x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7, p. 46.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.explanation: $\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta)\to\mathbb P(P=x)=0$ by continuity of measure along the decreasing sets, and `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le`.

MLMC_Allocation.definition_title: Optimal sample allocation: $\sum_{i\in s}\sqrt{V_iC_i}$, the Lagrange allocation and its rounding up
MLMC_Allocation.natural_language_statement:
These three definitions describe the optimal allocation of Monte Carlo samples among a finite family of independent estimators, the calculation behind the cost formula (1.1) of Giles (2015) and eq. (8) and (12) of Haas–Giles (2025). Let $\iota$ be an index type, $s\subseteq\iota$ a finite set of indices, and $V,C:\iota\to\mathbb{R}$, where $V_i$ is the variance and $C_i$ the cost of one sample of estimator $i$; let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be a variance target.

**`sumSqrtVC`.** The real number

$$
S(s,V,C)=\sum_{i\in s}\sqrt{V_i\,C_i},
$$

where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the real square root (which is $0$ at negative arguments); for $s=\emptyset$ it is $0$.

**`lagrangeN`.** For $i\in\iota$, the real number

$$
n^\star_i=\mathrm{lagrangeN}(s,V,C,\tau,i)=\tau^{-1}\sqrt{V_i/C_i}\;S(s,V,C),
$$

the Lagrange-multiplier allocation $N_i=\mu\sqrt{V_i/C_i}$ with $\mu=\tau^{-1}\sum_{j\in s}\sqrt{V_jC_j}$. It is defined for every $i\in\iota$, not only for $i\in s$, with Lean's conventions $0^{-1}=0$ and $x/0=0$.

**`optimalN`.** For $i\in\iota$, the natural number

$$
N_i=\mathrm{optimalN}(s,V,C,\tau,i)=\big\lceil n^\star_i\big\rceil_+,
$$

where $\lceil x\rceil_+$ is the least natural number $\ge x$, so that $\lceil x\rceil_+=0$ for $x\le0$. In particular $N_i=0$ whenever $\tau\le0$, $S(s,V,C)=0$ (for instance $s=\emptyset$) or $V_i/C_i\le0$. If $\tau>0$, $s\neq\emptyset$ and $V_j>0$, $C_j>0$ for all $j\in s$ and for $j=i$, then $N_i\ge1$.

With the variance target $\tau$, the allocation $n^\star$ minimises the total cost $\sum_{i\in s}n_iC_i$ subject to the total variance $\sum_{i\in s}V_i/n_i\le\tau$, and its cost is $\tau^{-1}S^2$. Rounding up to an integer follows Giles' proof of Theorem 1 ("the optimal value is rounded up to the nearest integer"). With the levels $\{0,\dots,L\}$ as index set and $\tau=\varepsilon^2$ this is the allocation of Giles (2015, §1.3) and of Haas–Giles (2025, §2.1); Giles' proof of Theorem 1 uses $\tau=\varepsilon^2/2$, and the nested estimator of Haas–Giles (§2.2) uses the index set $\{0,\dots,L\}\times\{\text{low precision},\text{correction}\}$.
MLMC_Allocation.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §1.3, p. 4 of the author's version (the unnumbered allocation N_ℓ = μ√(V_ℓ/C_ℓ), μ = ε⁻²Σ√(V_ℓC_ℓ), leading to eq. (1.1)) and §2.1, p. 7 (rounding up to an integer in the proof sketch of Theorem 1); I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §2.1, p. 3 (N_ℓ = λ√(V_ℓ/C_ℓ), λ = ε⁻²Σ√(V_ℓC_ℓ), leading to eq. (8)) and §2.2, p. 4 (λ_M, leading to eq. (12)). The general finite index set and variance target τ are the formalization's.

MLMC_Complexity.definition_title: Giles (2015), Theorem 1: the three-regime complexity bound, the rate functions and the proof constants
MLMC_Complexity.natural_language_statement:
These definitions are the objects of the real-analysis core of Giles' MLMC complexity theorem (Giles 2015, Theorem 1). All parameters are real numbers, levels $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ are cast to $\mathbb{R}$ in exponents, $2^{x}$ and $\varepsilon^{x}$ with real $x$ are real powers, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

**`complexityBound`.** For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$,

$$
\mathrm{complexityBound}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\varepsilon)=\begin{cases}\varepsilon^{-2}, & \gamma<\beta,\\ \varepsilon^{-2}\,(\log\varepsilon)^2, & \beta=\gamma,\\ \varepsilon^{-2-(\gamma-\beta)/\alpha}, & \beta<\gamma.\end{cases}
$$

The cases are tested in this order, so the last one is exactly $\beta<\gamma$. The theorems use it only for $\alpha>0$ and $0<\varepsilon<e^{-1}$; outside this range Mathlib's conventions apply (real powers of $\varepsilon\le0$, $\log0=0$, $\log x=\log|x|$, and $(\gamma-\beta)/0=0$).

**`Vb` and `Cb`.** For $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$,

$$
\mathrm{Vb}(\beta,c_2,\ell)=c_2\,2^{-\beta\ell},\qquad \mathrm{Cb}(\gamma,c_3,\ell)=c_3\,2^{\gamma\ell}.
$$

**`levelL`.** For $\alpha,c_1,\delta\in\mathbb{R}$, the natural number

$$
\mathrm{levelL}(\alpha,c_1,\delta)=\Big\lceil\frac{\log_2(c_1/\delta)}{\alpha}\Big\rceil_+,
$$

where $\log_2x=\log x/\log2$ and $\lceil x\rceil_+$ is the least natural number $\ge x$. The value is $0$ when $\log_2(c_1/\delta)/\alpha\le0$, and also when $\alpha=0$ or $\delta=0$ (by $x/0=0$ and $\log0=0$). For $\alpha,c_1,\delta>0$ it is the least $L\in\mathbb{N}$ with $c_1\,2^{-\alpha L}\le\delta$.

**`K1` and `K2`.** The constants

$$
K_1(\alpha,c_1)=2^{\alpha}\,(1+2c_1),\qquad K_2(\alpha,c_1)=\frac{|\log(2c_1)|+1}{\alpha\log2}+2.
$$

`complexityBound` is the three-case bound of Theorem 1, $\mathbb{E}[C]\le c_4\varepsilon^{-2}$ for $\beta>\gamma$, $c_4\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2$ for $\beta=\gamma$ and $c_4\varepsilon^{-2-(\gamma-\beta)/\alpha}$ for $\beta<\gamma$. `Vb` and `Cb` are the right-hand sides of its conditions iii) $V_\ell\le c_2 2^{-\beta\ell}$ and iv) $C_\ell\le c_3 2^{\gamma\ell}$. `levelL`, `K1` and `K2` are formalization devices for Giles' proof sketch: the finest level is $L=\mathrm{levelL}(\alpha,c_1,\varepsilon/2)$, so that the bias bound $c_1 2^{-\alpha L}$ of condition i) is at most $\varepsilon/2$, and for $\alpha,c_1>0$ and $0<\varepsilon<e^{-1}$ this level satisfies $2^{\alpha L}\le K_1/\varepsilon$ and $L+1\le K_2\,|\log\varepsilon|$.
MLMC_Complexity.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.1, Theorem 1 (pp. 6–7 of the author's version): the bound on E[C] in the three regimes β > γ, β = γ, β < γ (complexityBound) and conditions iii), iv) (Vb, Cb). levelL, K1 and K2 are formalization devices for the proof sketch on p. 7 (choice of the finest level L; the formalization splits the error as bias ≤ ε/2 and variance ≤ ε²/2).

MLMC_StandardEstimator.definition_title: Giles (2015), eq. (2.2): the standard MLMC estimator built from random inputs, and its total cost
MLMC_StandardEstimator.natural_language_statement:
These definitions construct Giles' standard multilevel Monte Carlo estimator (2.2) from random inputs. Let $\Omega_0$ be the space of one random input (for an SDE, a Brownian path), $\Omega$ the space on which the simulation runs, and $P_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$ ($\ell\in\mathbb{N}$) the level-$\ell$ approximations. The inputs are a family of maps $\omega^{(\ell,n)}:\Omega\to\Omega_0$ indexed by $(\ell,n)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$: the $n$-th sample on level $\ell$ is computed from the input $\omega^{(\ell,n)}$. The definitions involve no measurability or probability structure.

They use the level-$\ell$ correction $\Delta P_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$, $P_{-1}\equiv0$ (`levelDiff`, defined in the bundle `MLMC_LevelDiff`).

**`levelEstimator`.** For a level $\ell$ and a sample number $N\in\mathbb{N}$, the function on $\Omega$

$$
Y_\ell(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta P_\ell\big(\omega^{(\ell,n)}(x)\big),
$$

with the samples numbered $0,\dots,N-1$ (the paper's $1,\dots,N_\ell$). For $N=0$ the sum is empty and Lean's convention $0^{-1}=0$ gives $Y_\ell=0$.

**`mlmcEstimator`.** For a finest level $L\in\mathbb{N}$ and sample numbers $N:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, the function on $\Omega$

$$
Y(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}Y_\ell(x),
$$

where $Y_\ell$ is the level-$\ell$ estimator with $N_\ell$ samples.

**`totalCost`.** Given the cost $\mathrm{cost}_{\ell,n}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ of the $n$-th sample on level $\ell$ (a random quantity), the function on $\Omega$

$$
C(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\ \sum_{n=0}^{N_\ell-1}\mathrm{cost}_{\ell,n}(x).
$$

The first two definitions are the estimator (2.2), $Y=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}Y_\ell$ with $Y_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N_\ell}\big(P^{(\ell,n)}_\ell-P^{(\ell,n)}_{\ell-1}\big)$ and $P_{-1}\equiv0$, in which the fine and the coarse approximation of one sample use the same input and "independent samples are used at each level of correction"; independence and a common law of the inputs are imposed later, as hypotheses on the maps $\omega^{(\ell,n)}$. `totalCost` formalises the computational cost $C$ whose expectation Theorem 1 bounds. The paper gives no formula for $C$; the sum of the per-sample costs is the formalization's reading, and its mean is the overall cost $\sum_{\ell}N_\ell C_\ell$ of §1.3 when each sample on level $\ell$ has expected cost $C_\ell$.
MLMC_StandardEstimator.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.1, eq. (2.2) (p. 6 of the author's version); §1.3, p. 4 (the same estimator, "independent samples are used at each level of correction", and the overall cost Σ N_ℓC_ℓ); the computational cost C of Theorem 1 (p. 7). totalCost is the formalization's reading of C, for which the paper gives no formula.

MLMC_Randomised.definition_title: Giles (2015), §2.2: the single-term randomised MLMC estimator ($1$ and $N$ samples) and its level distributions
MLMC_Randomised.natural_language_statement:
These definitions formalise the randomised ("single-term") multilevel estimator of Rhee and Glynn, as presented by Giles (2015, §2.2), and two choices of its level distribution.

**`singleTerm`.** Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $P_\ell:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ ($\ell\in\mathbb{N}$) the level approximations, $K:\Omega\to\mathbb{N}$ a random level and $p:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ the level probabilities. The single-term estimator is

$$
Y(\omega)=\frac{1}{p_{K(\omega)}}\,\Delta P_{K(\omega)}(\omega),
$$

where $\Delta P_0=P_0$ and $\Delta P_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ for $\ell\ge1$ (the correction of the standard estimator, with $P_{-1}\equiv0$). If $p_{K(\omega)}=0$, Lean's convention $0^{-1}=0$ gives $Y(\omega)=0$.

**`singleTermN`.** For a second sample space $\Omega'$, maps $\xi_n:\Omega'\to\Omega$ ($n\in\mathbb{N}$), the $n$-th of which produces the $n$-th sample (a path together with its level), and $N\in\mathbb{N}$, the average of $N$ samples

$$
Y_N(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}Y\big(\xi_n(x)\big)\qquad(x\in\Omega'),
$$

with the samples numbered $0,\dots,N-1$ (the paper's $1,\dots,N$); for $N=0$ it is $0$.

**`geomLevelProb`.** For $\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ and $r=2^{-(\beta+\gamma)/2}$ (a real power),

$$
p_\ell=(1-r)\,r^{\ell}\qquad(\ell\in\mathbb{N}).
$$

If $\beta+\gamma>0$ then $0<r<1$, so $p_\ell>0$ and $\sum_{\ell\ge0}p_\ell=1$: it is the geometric distribution with $p_\ell\propto2^{-(\beta+\gamma)\ell/2}$. If $\beta+\gamma\le0$ all values are $\le0$ and it is not a probability distribution.

**`optimalLevelProb`.** For $V,C:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ (the variances $V_\ell$ and costs $C_\ell$ of the levels),

$$
p_\ell=\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}\,\Big(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sqrt{V_k/C_k}\Big)^{-1}.
$$

The series is Mathlib's unconditional sum, which is $0$ when the series is not summable; with $x/0=0$ every $p_\ell$ is then $0$. Also $V_\ell/C_\ell=0$ if $C_\ell=0$, and the real square root vanishes at negative arguments.

`singleTerm` is one sample and `singleTermN` the full estimator $Y=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_{\ell^{(n)}}^{-1}\big(P^{(n)}_{\ell^{(n)}}-P^{(n)}_{\ell^{(n)}-1}\big)$, written with a random level $\ell'$ as $p_{\ell'}^{-1}(P_{\ell'}-P_{\ell'-1})$ in Giles' unbiasedness computation. `geomLevelProb` is Giles' choice $p_\ell\propto2^{-(\gamma+\beta)\ell/2}$ for $\beta>\gamma$, which makes $\sum_\ell p_\ell^{-1}V_\ell$ and $\sum_\ell p_\ell C_\ell$ finite under the conditions of Theorem 1; the normalising factor $1-r$ is the formalization's. `optimalLevelProb` is Giles' optimal choice $p_\ell=\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}\,\big(\sum_{\ell'}\sqrt{V_{\ell'}/C_{\ell'}}\big)^{-1}$.
MLMC_Randomised.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.2 (pp. 9–10 of the author's version), presenting the estimator of Rhee and Glynn (2012, 2013): the estimator Y (p. 9) and p_{ℓ'}⁻¹(P_{ℓ'} − P_{ℓ'−1}) (p. 10), the choice p_ℓ ∝ 2^{−(γ+β)ℓ/2} (p. 10) and the optimal p_ℓ = √(V_ℓ/C_ℓ)(Σ_{ℓ'}√(V_{ℓ'}/C_{ℓ'}))⁻¹ (p. 10). The normalisation 1 − 2^{−(β+γ)/2} in geomLevelProb is the formalization's.

MLMC_MultiIndex.natural_language_statement:
In multi-index Monte Carlo (MIMC) the level is a multi-index $\boldsymbol{\ell}=(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_D)\in\mathbb{N}^D$. For a real-valued function $\boldsymbol{\ell}\mapsto P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}$ on $\mathbb{N}^D$ (in the formalization it is applied both to the values of random variables at a fixed outcome and to expectations), the backward difference in direction $d$ is $\Delta_dP_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}=P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}-P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}-\mathbf{e}_d}$, where $\mathbf{e}_d$ is the $d$-th unit vector and $P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}-\mathbf{e}_d}$ is read as $0$ when $\ell_d=0$.

**`crossDiff`.** The cross-difference

$$
\boldsymbol{\Delta}P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}=\Big(\prod_{d=1}^{D}\Delta_d\Big)P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}=\sum_{S}(-1)^{|S|}\,P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}-\sum_{d\in S}\mathbf{e}_d},
$$

where $S$ runs over the subsets of $\{1,\dots,D\}$ with $\ell_d\ge1$ for all $d\in S$. It is defined by recursion on $D$: for $D=0$ there is a single multi-index and $\boldsymbol{\Delta}P=P$; with $D+1$ directions, writing $\boldsymbol{\ell}=(\ell_1,\boldsymbol{\ell}')$ and $\boldsymbol{\Delta}'$ for the cross-difference in the remaining $D$ directions,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Delta}P_{(\ell_1,\boldsymbol{\ell}')}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\big[P_{(\ell_1,\cdot)}\big]_{\boldsymbol{\ell}'}-\begin{cases}0, & \ell_1=0,\\ \boldsymbol{\Delta}'\big[P_{(\ell_1-1,\cdot)}\big]_{\boldsymbol{\ell}'}, & \ell_1\ge1.\end{cases}
$$

For $D=1$ it is the MLMC correction $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ with $P_{-1}\equiv0$; for $D=2$, for example, $\boldsymbol{\Delta}P_{(5,4)}=P_{(5,4)}-P_{(4,4)}-P_{(5,3)}+P_{(4,3)}$, the four evaluations marked in Giles' Figure 2.1.

The cross-differences are the terms of the MIMC telescoping sum $\mathbb{E}[P]=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\ell}\ge\mathbf{0}}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Delta}P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}]$ and appear in condition iii) $\mathbb{E}[Y_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}]=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Delta}P_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}]$ of Theorem 2; summed over a box $\{\boldsymbol{\ell}:\ell_d\le k_d\text{ for all }d\}$ they give $P_{\mathbf{k}}$.
MLMC_MultiIndex.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.4 (pp. 12–13 of the author's version): the backward difference Δ_dP_ℓ ≡ P_ℓ − P_{ℓ−e_d}, the cross-difference ΔP_ℓ ≡ (∏_{d=1}^D Δ_d)P_ℓ and Figure 2.1, after Haji-Ali, Nobile and Tempone (2014a). Reading P as 0 at indices with a negative entry extends the paper's convention P_{−1} ≡ 0 (stated for one-dimensional levels) to every direction; the recursive definition is the formalization's.

MLMC_Lattice.definition_title: MIMC lattice notation: $a\cdot\boldsymbol\ell$, boxes, critical directions, index set $\theta\cdot\boldsymbol\ell\le L$
MLMC_Lattice.natural_language_statement:
These definitions provide the notation for lattice sums over multi-indices $\boldsymbol{\ell}=(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_D)\in\mathbb{N}^D$ in the proof of the multi-index Monte Carlo (MIMC) complexity theorem (Giles 2015, Theorem 2). Here $D\in\mathbb{N}$ is the number of directions.

**`dot`.** For $a\in\mathbb{R}^D$ and $\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D$, the real number

$$
a\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}a_d\,\ell_d,
$$

which is $0$ when $D=0$.

**`box`.** For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the finite set $\mathrm{box}(D,n)=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}^D=\{\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D:\ell_d<n\text{ for all }d\}$. It is empty when $n=0$ and $D\ge1$; for $D=0$ it is the one-point set $\mathbb{N}^0$.

**`crit`.** For $\delta\in\mathbb{R}^D$, the natural number $\mathrm{crit}(\delta)=\#\{d\in\{1,\dots,D\}:\delta_d=0\}$, the number of "critical" directions.

**`indexSet`.** For $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^D$ and $L\in\mathbb{R}$, the finite set

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta,L)=\big\{\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D:\ \ell_d\le\lfloor L/\theta_d\rfloor_+\text{ for all }d,\ \ \theta\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}\le L\big\},
$$

where $\lfloor x\rfloor_+$ is the greatest natural number $\le x$ for $x\ge0$ and $0$ for $x<0$. When all $\theta_d>0$ the first condition follows from the second, so $\mathcal{L}(\theta,L)=\{\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D:\theta\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}\le L\}$, which is empty for $L<0$. If some $\theta_d\le0$, the first condition genuinely restricts $\ell_d$ (with Lean's convention $x/0=0$).

**`boxSize`.** The natural number

$$
\mathrm{boxSize}(\theta,L)=\sum_{d=1}^{D}\big(\lfloor L/\theta_d\rfloor_++1\big).
$$

Each summand is at most the total, so $\mathcal{L}(\theta,L)\subseteq\mathrm{box}(D,\mathrm{boxSize}(\theta,L))$.

`indexSet` is the MIMC summation region, which Giles describes as being "of the form $\boldsymbol{\ell}\cdot\mathbf{n}\le L$ for a particular choice of direction vector $\mathbf{n}$ with strictly positive components" (a triangle in two dimensions, Figure 2.2), and `dot` is the pairing in the exponents $\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $\beta\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $\gamma\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}$ of conditions ii), iv), v) of Theorem 2. `box`, `crit` and `boxSize` are formalization devices: lattice sums are written as finite sums over boxes with bounds uniform in the box size, and the number $m=\mathrm{crit}(\delta)$ of directions with $\delta_d=0$ determines the polynomial factor $(1+L)^{m-1}$ in these bounds (in the proof of Theorem 2, $m$ is the number $D_2$ of directions attaining $\eta$).
MLMC_Lattice.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.4: Theorem 2 (pp. 13–14 of the author's version; the pairings α·ℓ, β·ℓ, γ·ℓ) and p. 15 (the summation region "of the form ℓ·n ≤ L", Figure 2.2). box, crit and boxSize are formalization devices for the lattice-point counting in the proof of Theorem 2, which the paper does not give.

MLMC_Theorem2.definition_title: Giles (2015), Theorem 2: the MIMC exponent $\eta$, the counts $D_2$, $D_3$ and the three-regime cost bound
MLMC_Theorem2.natural_language_statement:
These definitions are the quantities in the conclusion of Giles' formulation of the multi-index Monte Carlo (MIMC) complexity theorem (Giles 2015, Theorem 2). For `mimcEta` and `mimcD2`, $D\ge1$ is the number of directions (the Lean type class `NeZero D`), and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^D$ are the rate vectors of conditions ii) $|\mathbb{E}[Y_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}]|\le c_1 2^{-\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}}$, iv) $V_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\le c_2 2^{-\beta\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}}$ and v) $C_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\le c_3 2^{\gamma\cdot\boldsymbol{\ell}}$.

**`mimcEta`.** The real number

$$
\eta=\max_{1\le d\le D}\frac{\gamma_d-\beta_d}{\alpha_d},
$$

with Lean's convention $x/0=0$ if some $\alpha_d=0$ (the theorems assume $\alpha_d>0$).

**`mimcD2`.** The natural number $D_2=\#\{d\in\{1,\dots,D\}:(\gamma_d-\beta_d)/\alpha_d=\eta\}$, the number of directions attaining the maximum; $D_2\ge1$.

**`mimcD3`.** For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^D$ (any $D\in\mathbb{N}$), the natural number $D_3=\#\{d\in\{1,\dots,D\}:\alpha_d=\tfrac12\beta_d\}$, the number of directions in which the condition $\alpha_d\ge\tfrac12\beta_d$ of Theorem 2 holds with equality. It is not a quantity of the paper: it enters the logarithmic exponents proved here for the case $\alpha_d=\tfrac12\beta_d$ for some $d$, which the paper leaves open.

**`mimcBound`.** For $\eta,e_1,e_2,\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$,

$$
\mathrm{mimcBound}(\eta,e_1,e_2,\varepsilon)=\begin{cases}\varepsilon^{-2}, & \eta<0,\\ \varepsilon^{-2}\,|\log\varepsilon|^{e_1}, & \eta=0,\\ \varepsilon^{-2-\eta}\,|\log\varepsilon|^{e_2}, & \eta>0,\end{cases}
$$

where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and all powers are real powers (the exponents $e_1,e_2$ are real numbers). The theorems use it for $0<\varepsilon<e^{-1}$, where $|\log\varepsilon|>1$.

Theorem 2 bounds the expected cost of the MIMC estimator by $c_4\,\mathrm{mimcBound}(\eta,e_1,e_2,\varepsilon)$ and states that $e_1=2D_2$ and $e_2=(D_2-1)(2+\eta)$ when $\alpha_d>\tfrac12\beta_d$ for all $d$; the paper leaves the exponents unspecified when $\alpha_d=\tfrac12\beta_d$ for some $d$, where the formal version uses $e_1=2D_2+(D_3-3)^+$ and $e_2=(D_2-1)(2+\eta)+(D_3-1)^+$ with $x^+=\max(x,0)$.
MLMC_Theorem2.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.4, Theorem 2 (pp. 13–14 of the author's version): η = max_d (γ_d − β_d)/α_d, D₂ = the number of dimensions d with (γ_d − β_d)/α_d = η, and the bound on E[C] for η < 0, η = 0, η > 0; Giles' formulation of the MIMC theorem of Haji-Ali, Nobile and Tempone (2014a). D₃ (mimcD3, the number of directions with α_d = ½β_d) is a formalization device, not a quantity of the paper: it appears in the exponents proved for the case α_d = ½β_d that the paper leaves open ('The form of the exponents is more complicated when α_d = ½β_d for some d', p. 14).

MLMC_Nested.definition_title: Nested MLMC (Haas–Giles 2025, §2.2): the index set, the two sample kinds, the nested estimator and its cost
MLMC_Nested.natural_language_statement:
In the nested multilevel Monte Carlo framework of Haas and Giles, each level $\ell\in\{0,\dots,L\}$ carries two Monte Carlo estimators: one of the low-precision term $\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell]$ and one of the correction $\mathbb{E}[\Delta P_\ell-\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell]$ (eq. (9)). These definitions index the $2(L+1)$ estimators by a single finite set, so that results for a finite family of independent estimators apply to the nested estimator.

**`nIdx`.** For $L\in\mathbb{N}$, the finite set

$$
\mathrm{nIdx}(L)=\{0,1,\dots,L\}\times\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathrm{Bool},
$$

with $2(L+1)$ elements; the index $(\ell,\mathrm{true})$ stands for the low-precision term $\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell$ and $(\ell,\mathrm{false})$ for the correction $\Delta P_\ell-\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell$.

**`pairFam`.** For two level-indexed families $f,g:\mathbb{N}\to X$ with values in an arbitrary type $X$, the family on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathrm{Bool}$

$$
\mathrm{pairFam}(f,g)(\ell,b)=\begin{cases}f(\ell), & b=\mathrm{true},\\ g(\ell), & b=\mathrm{false}.\end{cases}
$$

The simp lemmas `pairFam_true` and `pairFam_false` state these two cases.

When $X$ carries an addition (for instance $X=\mathbb{R}$, or real-valued random variables), the sum of $\mathrm{pairFam}(f,g)$ over $\mathrm{nIdx}(L)$ equals $\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\big(f(\ell)+g(\ell)\big)$, the shape of the nested cost (10) and variance (11), with $f,g$ the low-precision and correction variances, costs, sample numbers or estimators. These two definitions are formalization devices, not objects of the paper.

The remaining definitions build the nested estimator from random inputs. Let $\Omega_0$ be the space of one random input, $\Omega$ the space on which the simulation runs, $P_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$ the level approximations with corrections $\Delta P_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ ($P_{-1}\equiv0$, `levelDiff`), and $\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$ the low-precision level differences.

**`nestedTerm`.** The family on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathrm{Bool}$ of the quantities sampled: $(\ell,\mathrm{true})\mapsto\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell$ and $(\ell,\mathrm{false})\mapsto\Delta P_\ell-\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell$, i.e. $\mathrm{pairFam}\big(\widetilde{\Delta P},\ \ell\mapsto\Delta P_\ell-\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell\big)$ (simp lemmas `nestedTerm_true`, `nestedTerm_false`).

**`nestedEstimator`.** For inputs $\omega^{((\ell,b),n)}:\Omega\to\Omega_0$ indexed by $((\ell,b),n)\in(\mathbb{N}\times\mathrm{Bool})\times\mathbb{N}$, a finest level $L$ and sample numbers $\widetilde{N},N^\Delta:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, the function on $\Omega$

$$
Y(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\Big(\frac{1}{\widetilde{N}_\ell}\sum_{n=0}^{\widetilde{N}_\ell-1}\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell\big(\omega^{((\ell,\mathrm{true}),n)}(x)\big)+\frac{1}{N^\Delta_\ell}\sum_{n=0}^{N^\Delta_\ell-1}\big(\Delta P_\ell-\widetilde{\Delta P}_\ell\big)\big(\omega^{((\ell,\mathrm{false}),n)}(x)\big)\Big),
$$

the sum over the levels of the Monte Carlo averages (`blockMean`) of the two kinds of samples, each sample computed from its own input; an empty average ($\widetilde{N}_\ell=0$ or $N^\Delta_\ell=0$) is $0$. This is the estimator of the split (9).

**`nestedCost`.** Given the costs $\widetilde{\mathrm{cost}}_{\ell,n},\mathrm{cost}^\Delta_{\ell,n}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ of the $n$-th low-precision and correction sample on level $\ell$, the total cost

$$
C(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\Big(\sum_{n=0}^{\widetilde{N}_\ell-1}\widetilde{\mathrm{cost}}_{\ell,n}(x)+\sum_{n=0}^{N^\Delta_\ell-1}\mathrm{cost}^\Delta_{\ell,n}(x)\Big),
$$

whose mean is the nested cost (10) when the samples have expected costs $\widetilde{C}_\ell$ and $C^\Delta_\ell$. The paper gives no formula for the estimator or its cost; these are the formalization's reading of (9) and (10).
MLMC_Nested.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §2.2, eq. (9)–(12) (p. 4): the split E[ΔP_ℓ] = E[Δ̃P_ℓ] + E[ΔP_ℓ − Δ̃P_ℓ] estimated with Ñ_ℓ and N^Δ_ℓ samples, and the cost (10). nIdx and pairFam are formalization devices, and the explicit estimator and cost are the formalization's reading of (9) and (10); the paper does not define these objects.

MLMC_LevelDiff.definition_title: Giles (2015), §1.3 and (2.2): the multilevel correction $\Delta P_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$, $P_{-1}\equiv0$
MLMC_LevelDiff.natural_language_statement:
Let $\Omega_0$ be a type (for instance the space of one random input) and $P_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$ ($\ell\in\mathbb{N}$) the level-$\ell$ approximations of a quantity of interest.

**`levelDiff`.** The level-$\ell$ correction $\Delta P_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$,

$$
\Delta P_0=P_0,\qquad \Delta P_{\ell+1}=P_{\ell+1}-P_\ell\quad(\ell\in\mathbb{N}),
$$

that is, $\Delta P_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ with the convention $P_{-1}\equiv0$. The simp lemmas `levelDiff_zero` and `levelDiff_succ` are these two equations.

This is the correction of the multilevel identity $\mathbb{E}[P_L]=\mathbb{E}[P_0]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}[P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}]$ of Giles (2015), §1.3, and of the estimator (2.2), where the paper writes $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ with "$P_{-1}\equiv0$". Haas and Giles (2025, §2.1) use the same $\Delta P_\ell$. The definition involves no measurability or probability structure.
MLMC_LevelDiff.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §1.3, p. 4 of the author's version (the identity E[P_L] = E[P_0] + Σ_{ℓ=1}^{L} E[P_ℓ − P_{ℓ−1}]) and §2.1, eq. (2.2) (P_{−1} ≡ 0); I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §2.1, eq. (3) (p. 3)

MLMC_SampleMean.definition_title: Giles (2015), §1.1: the Monte Carlo average of $N$ samples over a block of inputs
MLMC_SampleMean.natural_language_statement:
Every estimator in multilevel Monte Carlo is a sum of Monte Carlo averages, each over its own block of random inputs. Let $\iota$ be an index type (the blocks, for instance the levels), $\Omega_0$ the space of one random input and $\Omega$ the space on which the simulation runs. Let $f_i:\Omega_0\to\mathbb{R}$ ($i\in\iota$) be the quantities to average and $\omega^{(i,n)}:\Omega\to\Omega_0$, indexed by $(i,n)\in\iota\times\mathbb{N}$, the inputs: the $n$-th sample of block $i$ is computed from $\omega^{(i,n)}$.

**`blockMean`.** For a block $i\in\iota$ and a sample number $N\in\mathbb{N}$, the function on $\Omega$

$$
\bar f_{i,N}(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f_i\big(\omega^{(i,n)}(x)\big),
$$

the Monte Carlo average of $f_i$ over the inputs $\omega^{(i,0)},\dots,\omega^{(i,N-1)}$ (the paper numbers them $1,\dots,N$). For $N=0$ the sum is empty and Lean's convention $0^{-1}=0$ gives $\bar f_{i,0}=0$.

This is the "simple Monte Carlo estimate", "an average of values $P(\omega)$ for $N$ independent samples", of Giles (2015), §1.1, with its "variance $N^{-1}\mathbb{V}[P]$" when the inputs are independent with a common law; independence and the law of the inputs are imposed later, as hypotheses on the maps $\omega^{(i,n)}$. The standard estimator (2.2) is the case $f_\ell=\Delta P_\ell$, and the nested estimator of Haas and Giles (2025) uses the blocks $\{0,\dots,L\}\times\{\text{low precision},\text{correction}\}$. The definition involves no measurability or probability structure.
MLMC_SampleMean.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §1.1, p. 2 of the author's version (the Monte Carlo average of N independent samples and its variance N⁻¹V[P]) and §1.3, p. 4 (\"independent samples are used at each level of correction\"). The indexing by blocks is the formalization's.

MLMC_ControlVariate.definition_title: Giles (2015), §1.2: the correlation $\rho=\mathrm{Cov}[f,g]/\sqrt{\mathbb V[f]\,\mathbb V[g]}$ of two random variables
MLMC_ControlVariate.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §1.2, states the optimal control variate in terms of "the correlation between $f$ and $g$". Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable space, $\mu$ a measure on it and $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.

**`correlation`.** The real number

$$
\rho(f,g)=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}[f,g]}{\sqrt{\mathbb V[f]\,\mathbb V[g]}},
$$

where $\mathrm{Cov}[f,g]=\int_\Omega\big(f-\mathbb E[f]\big)\big(g-\mathbb E[g]\big)\,d\mu$ is Mathlib's `covariance` and $\mathbb V$ is Mathlib's `variance`, with $\mathbb E[h]=\int_\Omega h\,d\mu$ the Bochner integral.

This is the usual correlation coefficient when $\mu$ is a probability measure and $f,g$ are square-integrable with positive variances, which is how every theorem uses it. In the degenerate case $\mathbb V[f]\,\mathbb V[g]=0$ the square root is $0$ and Lean's convention $x/0=0$ gives $\rho=0$; no theorem relies on that value.
MLMC_ControlVariate.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §1.2, p. 3 of the author's version ("where ρ is the correlation between f and g").

MLMC_ErrorAnalysis.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.3, measures how reliable an empirical variance is by the kurtosis of the multilevel correction. Let $(\Omega_0,\mathcal F_0)$ be a measurable space with a measure $\nu$ and $X:\Omega_0\to\mathbb R$.

**`kurtosis`.** The real number

$$
\kappa(X)=\frac{\int X^4\,d\nu}{\big(\int X^2\,d\nu\big)^2}.
$$

For a random variable with zero mean this is the usual kurtosis $\mathbb E[X^4]/(\mathbb E[X^2])^2$, the definition the paper states. The integrals are Bochner integrals (with the value $0$ for a non-integrable integrand) and Lean's $x/0=0$ applies when $\int X^2\,d\nu=0$; the theorems that use $\kappa$ assume $\int X^2\,d\nu>0$ and $\int X^4\,d\nu<\infty$ where it matters.
MLMC_ErrorAnalysis.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.3, p. 23 of the author's version ("the kurtosis κ is defined as κ = E[X⁴]/(E[X²])²").

MLMC_Corrections.definition_title: Giles (2015), §2.1: level corrections $P^f_\ell-P^c_{\ell-1}$ (fine and coarse approximations) and $\tfrac12(P_\ell(\omega)+P_\ell(\omega_a))-P_{\ell-1}(\omega)$ (antithetic)
MLMC_Corrections.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.1, notes that "the multilevel theorem allows for the use of other estimators, provided they satisfy the restriction of condition ii)", and gives two examples of level corrections other than $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$. Let $\Omega_0$ be the space of one random input and let $P_\ell,P^f_\ell,P^c_\ell:\Omega_0\to\mathbb R$ ($\ell\in\mathbb N$) be approximations.

**`fineCoarseDiff`.** The correction with different fine and coarse approximations,

$$
\Delta^{fc}_0=P^f_0,\qquad\Delta^{fc}_\ell=P^f_\ell-P^c_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1),
$$

that is $P^f_\ell-P^c_{\ell-1}$ with the convention $P^c_{-1}\equiv0$. The paper's estimator is $Y_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_n\big(P^f_\ell(\omega^{(n)})-P^c_{\ell-1}(\omega^{(n)})\big)$.

**`antitheticDiff`.** For a map $a:\Omega_0\to\Omega_0$ producing the antithetic input $\omega_a=a(\omega)$, the antithetic correction

$$
\Delta^{a}_0(\omega)=\tfrac12\big(P_0(\omega)+P_0(a(\omega))\big),\qquad\Delta^{a}_\ell(\omega)=\tfrac12\big(P_\ell(\omega)+P_\ell(a(\omega))\big)-P_{\ell-1}(\omega)\quad(\ell\ge1),
$$

that is $\tfrac12(P_\ell(\omega)+P_\ell(\omega_a))-P_{\ell-1}(\omega)$ with $P_{-1}\equiv0$, the summand of the paper's antithetic estimator.

Both are plain functions of one input; no measurability or probability structure is involved in the definitions. The factor $\tfrac12$ is written $2^{-1}$.
MLMC_Corrections.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.1, pp. 8–9 of the author's version (the estimator with P^f_ℓ and P^c_{ℓ−1} and the identity (2.4); the antithetic estimator).

MLMC_Richardson.definition_title: Giles (2015), §2.3: the nodes $x_\ell=2^{-\alpha\ell}$ and the weights $w_\ell=\prod_{k\ne\ell}x_k/(x_k-x_\ell)$ of multilevel Richardson–Romberg extrapolation
MLMC_Richardson.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.3, presents the multilevel Richardson–Romberg (ML2R) extrapolation of Lemaire and Pagès (2013), which combines the level means $\mathbb E[P_\ell]$, $\ell=0,\dots,L$, with weights $w_\ell$ that cancel the terms $2^{-n\alpha\ell}$, $n=1,\dots,L$, of the weak-error expansion.

**`ml2rNode`.** For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $\ell\in\mathbb N$,

$$
x_\ell=2^{-\alpha\ell}\qquad(\text{real power}).
$$

**`ml2rWeight`.** For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $L,\ell\in\mathbb N$,

$$
w_\ell=\prod_{k\in\{0,\dots,L\}\setminus\{\ell\}}\frac{x_k}{x_k-x_\ell},
$$

the value at $0$ of the Lagrange basis polynomial of the node $x_\ell$ among $x_0,\dots,x_L$. For $\alpha>0$ the nodes are distinct and these are the weights of the paper (see `ml2r_weights`).

**Formalization Note** Both are total functions: division is Lean's field division (with $t/0=0$), which only matters when $\alpha=0$; for $\ell>L$ the product runs over all $k\le L$. The theorems assume $\alpha>0$ and use $\ell\le L$.
MLMC_Richardson.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.3, pp. 11–12 of the author's version (the weights of Lemaire and Pagès 2013).

MLMC_RoundingError.definition_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §4: fixed-point round-to-nearest $\tilde x=2^{e-d}\,\mathrm{round}(x/2^{e-d})$ and the error-variance bounds $V_{indep}$ (26) and $V_{corr}$ (27)
MLMC_RoundingError.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §4, model the rounding error of a low-precision fixed-point path simulation. A variable with exponent $e\in\mathbb Z$ and bit-width $d\in\mathbb N$ is stored as $\tilde x=(-1)^s2^{e-d}n$ with $0\le n<2^d$; results are rounded to nearest.

**`roundFixed`.** For $e\in\mathbb Z$, $d\in\mathbb N$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$
\tilde x=2^{e-d}\,\mathrm{round}\big(x/2^{e-d}\big),
$$

the nearest point of the grid $2^{e-d}\mathbb Z$ (Mathlib's `round`, which rounds half-integers up).

**`vIndep`.** For a finite index set $s$ of variables with mean-square sensitivities $M_i$ ($M_i=\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]$ in the paper), exponents $e_i\in\mathbb Z$ and bit-widths $d_i\in\mathbb N$,

$$
V_{indep}(d)=\frac1{12}\sum_{i\in s}M_i\,4^{e_i-d_i}\qquad\text{(26)}.
$$

**`vCorr`.** With the same data,

$$
V_{corr}(d)=\Big(\sum_{i\in s}\sqrt{M_i}\,2^{e_i-d_i-1}\Big)^2\qquad\text{(27)}.
$$

**Formalization Note** Powers with integer exponents are `zpow`; $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is `Real.sqrt` (which is $0$ on negative numbers; the theorems use $M_i=\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\ge0$).
MLMC_RoundingError.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §4.1–4.2, pp. 8–9 (the fixed-point format, (20), (26), (27)).

MLMC_BitWidth.definition_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §5–§6: the fixed-point cost models (30) and (31), and the variance bound (26) with real bit-widths
MLMC_BitWidth.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §5, model the cost of a fixed-point path simulation on an FPGA as a function of the bit-widths $d_i$ of its variables $x_i$, and §6 optimises the bit-widths.

**`opCost`** (the cost (30), after Lee et al. 2006). The multiplications are indexed by a finite set $\mathcal M$, the $k$-th multiplying the variables $x_{a(k)}$ and $x_{b(k)}$; the additions are indexed by a finite set $\mathcal S$, the $k$-th adding $x_{a'(k)}$ and $x_{b'(k)}$. For real bit-widths $d_i$,

$$
\tilde C(d)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal M}d_{a(k)}\,d_{b(k)}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal S}\max\big(d_{a'(k)},d_{b'(k)}\big)\qquad\text{(30)}.
$$

**`opCount`.** For a finite set of operations with operands $a(k),b(k)$, the number of operand slots filled by $x_i$: $\#\{k:a(k)=i\}+\#\{k:b(k)=i\}$. This is $M_i$ for the multiplications and $M'_i$ for the additions ("the number of multiplications (resp. additions) in which the variable $x_i$ is involved"); a square $x_ix_i$ counts twice.

**`sepCost`** (the cost (31)). For a finite set of variables and real weights $M_i,M'_i$,

$$
\tilde C(d)=\frac12\sum_iM_i\,d_i^2+\sum_iM'_i\,d_i\qquad\text{(31)}.
$$

**`vIndepR`** (the bound (26) with real bit-widths). For a finite set $s$ of variables, $E_i=\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]$ and exponents $e_i\in\mathbb Z$,

$$
V_{indep}(d)=\frac1{12}\sum_{i\in s}E_i\,4^{e_i-d_i},\qquad d_i\in\mathbb R.
$$

**Formalization Note** The operations are given by index sets with operand maps rather than by sets of pairs, so an operation may occur several times. $4^{e_i-d_i}$ with a real exponent is the real power.
MLMC_BitWidth.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §5 (p. 11, (30), (31)) and §4.2 (p. 9, (26)), as used in §6.1 (p. 12).

MLMC_RectangularMIMC.definition_title: Giles (2015), §2.4: the rectangular MIMC index set $\{\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D:\ \ell_d\le L_d\}$
MLMC_RectangularMIMC.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.4, p. 15, discusses rectangular summation regions for multi-index Monte Carlo (MIMC), "as illustrated on the left in Figure 2.2".

**`rectSet`**. For $D\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbf{L}=(L_1,\dots,L_D)\in\mathbb{N}^D$ (with $0\in\mathbb{N}$), the rectangle

$$
\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{L})=\{\boldsymbol{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^D:\ \ell_d\le L_d\text{ for }d=1,\dots,D\}=\prod_{d=1}^{D}\{0,1,\dots,L_d\},
$$

a finite set of multi-indices whose outermost point is $\mathbf{L}$.

**Formalization Note** Multi-indices are functions `Fin D → ℕ`, and the rectangle is the finite product set `Fintype.piFinset fun d => range (L d + 1)`.
MLMC_RectangularMIMC.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.4, p. 15 ("It might seem natural that the summation region L should be rectangular, as illustrated on the left in Figure 2.2").

MLMC_Algorithm.definition_title: Giles (2015), §3.1: the idealised MLMC algorithm (robust remaining-error estimate, sample counts, stopping level)
MLMC_Algorithm.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.1, Algorithm 1: "start with $L=2$, and initial target of $N_0$ samples on levels $\ell=0,1,2$; while extra samples need to be evaluated: evaluate extra samples on each level, compute/update estimates for $V_\ell$, define optimal $N_\ell$, test for weak convergence, if not converged, set $L:=L+1$, and initialise target $N_L$". The driver `mlmc.m` (§3.4) implements it with the robust estimate `rem` of the remaining error. These definitions describe the algorithm with the exact level means $m_\ell=\mathbb E[P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}]$ and variances $V_\ell$ in place of their sample estimates.

**`alg1Rem`** (the robust estimate of the remaining error; p. 21 and the line `rem = max(ml(L+1+range).*2.^(alpha*range))/(2^alpha-1)` with `range = -2:0`, p. 26). For a sequence $m:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $L\in\mathbb N$,

$$
\mathrm{rem}_L=\frac{\max\big(|m_L|,\ |m_{L-1}|\,2^{-\alpha},\ |m_{L-2}|\,2^{-2\alpha}\big)}{2^\alpha-1}
$$

(with natural-number subtraction in the indices).

**`alg1Init`** (the initial samples). $N_0$ samples on each of the levels $0,1,2$ and none on the others: $\mathrm{init}_\ell=N_0$ for $\ell\le2$, and $0$ otherwise.

**`alg1Samples`** (the sample counts). For $N_0\in\mathbb N$, $V,C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$, the number of samples on level $\ell$ after the passes with finest levels $2,\dots,L$: $N^{(0)}_\ell=\mathrm{init}_\ell$ and

$$
N^{(L+1)}_\ell=\max\Big(N^{(L)}_\ell,\ \mathbf 1[2\le L+1,\ \ell\le L+1]\,\Big\lceil 2\varepsilon^{-2}\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}\sum_{\ell'=0}^{L+1}\sqrt{V_{\ell'}C_{\ell'}}\Big\rceil\Big),
$$

that is, every pass tops each level up to its target (3.1) (the driver's `dNl = max(0, Ns-Nl)`). For $L\le1$ no pass has been made yet.

**`alg1Level`** (the stopping level). The least $L\ge2$ with $\mathrm{rem}_L\le\varepsilon/\sqrt2$, and $0$ if there is none: the driver adds a level while `rem > eps/sqrt(2)`.

**Formalization Note** The target (3.1) is `optimalN (range (L + 1)) V C (ε ^ 2 / 2) ℓ`, the rounded-up Lagrange allocation for the variance target $\varepsilon^2/2$ (`allocation_eq_3_1`). The stopping level is defined with `Nat.find`; the driver's extra test "if (almost) converged" always holds in the idealised algorithm, since one round of extra samples reaches every target.
MLMC_Algorithm.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.1 (Algorithm 1 and (3.1), p. 21) and §3.4 (the driver mlmc.m, pp. 23–26).

MLMC_ApproxNormal.definition_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §3: interval means, the uniform grid $u_j=2^{-d}j$, the LUT values (15), and the coupled uniform variable (17)
MLMC_ApproxNormal.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §3: the three inversion methods approximate the inverse normal CDF $\Phi^{-1}$ by functions that are constant on the uniform intervals $\mathcal I_j=[u_j,u_{j+1}]$, $u_j=2^{-d}j$, and couple the low-precision $d$-bit integer $j$ with a full-precision $D$-bit integer $J$ and uniform variable $U$.

**`intervalMean`**. For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, the mean of $f$ over $[a,b]$:
$$
\mathrm{mean}(f,a,b)=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(u)\,du .
$$

**`gridPt`**. For $d,j\in\mathbb N$, the grid point $u_j=2^{-d}j=j/2^d$ (a real number).

**`lutValue`** (the LUT value (15) of method 1, §3.1). For $f$ and $d,j\in\mathbb N$,
$$
Z_j=2^d\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f(u)\,du ,
$$
the mean of $f$ over $\mathcal I_j$ (in the paper, $f=\Phi^{-1}$).

**`coupledUniform`** (the coupled full-precision uniform variable (17), §3.2). For $\pi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and $d,D,J\in\mathbb N$, with $j=\lfloor J/2^{D-d}\rfloor$ (the leading $d$ bits of the $D$-bit integer $J$),
$$
U=2^{-d}\pi(j)+2^{-D}\Big(\big(J-2^{D-d}j\big)+\tfrac12\Big).
$$
With $\pi=\mathrm{id}$ this is the method-1 variable $U=2^{-D}(J+\frac12)$ of §3.1 (`coupledUniform_eq`).

**`coupledIndex`**. The integer index of $U$: $K=2^{D-d}\pi(j)+(J\bmod 2^{D-d})$, so that $U=2^{-D}(K+\frac12)$ (`coupledUniform_eq_index`).

**Formalization Note** All integrals are Mathlib's interval integrals `∫ u in a..b` for Lebesgue measure. In `coupledUniform` the division $\lfloor J/2^{D-d}\rfloor$ and the subtraction $D-d$ are those of $\mathbb N$; the rest is computed in $\mathbb R$.
MLMC_ApproxNormal.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §3.1 (pp. 5, (14)–(15) and $U=2^{-D}(J+\frac12)$) and §3.2 (p. 6, (17)).

MLMC_NestedMLMC.definition_title: Giles (2015), §9.1: the nested model $\nu\otimes\rho^{\otimes\mathbb N}$, inner means $A_M$, level approximations $P_\ell$, antithetic corrections $Y_\ell$ and the target $f(\mathbb E_W[g])$
MLMC_NestedMLMC.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §9.1: nested simulation estimates $\mathbb E_Z\big[f(\mathbb E_W[g(Z,W)])\big]$, where $Z$ is an outer random variable and $W$ an independent inner random variable. On level $\ell$ the inner expectation is replaced by the mean of $M_\ell=2^\ell$ inner samples, and the level correction is an antithetic difference.

Throughout, $\nu$ is a measure on a measurable space $\mathcal Z$ (the law of $Z$), $\rho$ a measure on a measurable space $\mathcal W$ (the law of $W$), $g:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal W\to\mathbb R$ and $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$.

**`innerMean`**. For $M\in\mathbb N$, $z\in\mathcal Z$ and a sequence $w=(w_0,w_1,\dots)$ in $\mathcal W$, the mean of the first $M$ inner samples:
$$
A_M(z,w)=\frac1M\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}g(z,w_m)
$$
(which is $0$ when $M=0$).

**`shiftSeq`**. For $M\in\mathbb N$ and a sequence $w$, the shifted sequence $m\mapsto w_{M+m}$. With $M=M_{\ell-1}$ it lists the second half of the level-$\ell$ inner samples, and $A_M(z,\mathrm{shift}_M w)$ is their mean $A'_M$.

**`nestedSign`**. For $M,m\in\mathbb N$: $s_m=1$ if $m<M$ and $s_m=-1$ otherwise.

**`innerLaw`**. The law $\rho^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ of an independent sequence of inner samples with law $\rho$: Mathlib's infinite product measure `Measure.infinitePi` of the constant family $\rho$.

**`nestedLaw`**. The joint law $\nu\otimes\rho^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ of the outer variable and the independent inner samples, on $\mathcal Z\times\mathcal W^{\mathbb N}$.

**`nestedP`**. The level-$\ell$ approximation $P_\ell(z,w)=f\big(A_{2^\ell}(z,w)\big)$.

**`nestedDelta`**. The antithetic level correction (one outer sample): $Y_0=P_0$ and, for $\ell\ge0$ with $M=2^\ell$,
$$
Y_{\ell+1}(z,w)=f\big(A_{2M}(z,w)\big)-\tfrac12f\big(A_M(z,w)\big)-\tfrac12f\big(A_M(z,\mathrm{shift}_Mw)\big).
$$

**`nestedTarget`**. The quantity of interest for one outer sample, as a function on $\mathcal Z\times\mathcal W^{\mathbb N}$ that does not depend on the inner samples:
$$
P(z,w)=f\Big(\int_{\mathcal W}g(z,v)\,d\rho(v)\Big).
$$
Its mean under $\nu\otimes\rho^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ is $\mathbb E_Z\big[f(\mathbb E_W[g(Z,W)])\big]$.

**Formalization Note** The outer and inner randomness are modelled directly on the product space $\mathcal Z\times\mathcal W^{\mathbb N}$ with the product law; any model with $Z$ and $W^{(0)},W^{(1)},\dots$ mutually independent, $Z\sim\nu$ and $W^{(m)}\sim\rho$ has this joint law. Samples are numbered from $0$.
MLMC_NestedMLMC.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §9.1, pp. 57–58 of the author's version (the quantity E_Z[f(E_W[g(Z,W)])], the nested MC estimator, M_ℓ = 2^ℓ inner samples, and the antithetic estimator Y_ℓ).

MLMC_EulerMaruyama.definition_title: Haas–Giles (2025), (2), (4)–(5): the Euler–Maruyama path, the coarse path with frozen coefficients, the coarse increments $(Z_{2k}+Z_{2k+1})/\sqrt2$ and the level approximations
MLMC_EulerMaruyama.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §2, and Giles (2015), §5.1: the solution of the SDE $dS_t=a(S_t,t)\,dt+b(S_t,t)\,dW_t$ is approximated by the Euler–Maruyama scheme, driven by independent standard normal increments $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$. The coarse path of a level-$\ell$ sample reuses the fine increments.

Throughout, $a,b:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are the drift and the volatility (as functions of the state and the time), $h\in\mathbb R$ is the step, $S_0\in\mathbb R$ the initial value, and $z=(z_0,z_1,\dots)$ a sequence of real numbers (the normal increments).

**`emPath`**. The Euler–Maruyama path (Haas–Giles (2) and (4)): $S_0=S_0$ and, with $t_i=ih$,
$$
S_{i+1}=S_i+a(S_i,t_i)\,h+b(S_i,t_i)\,\sqrt h\,z_i .
$$

**`pairAvg`**. The coarse increments: $\mathrm{pairAvg}(z)_k=(z_{2k}+z_{2k+1})/\sqrt2$.

**`emCoarsePath`**. The coarse path of Haas–Giles (5): at even indices $S^c_{2k}$ is the Euler–Maruyama path with step $2h$ driven by $\mathrm{pairAvg}(z)$ evaluated at $k$, and
$$
S^c_{2k+1}=S^c_{2k}+a(S^c_{2k},t_{2k})\,h+b(S^c_{2k},t_{2k})\,\sqrt h\,z_{2k}.
$$
(The theorems `emCoarsePath_succ` and `eq_emCoarsePath` show that this is exactly the sequence defined by the recursion (5).)

**`stdNormalSeq`**. The law $N(0,1)^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ of an independent sequence of standard normal increments: Mathlib's infinite product measure `Measure.infinitePi` of the constant family `gaussianReal 0 1`.

**`emFine`**. For $T\in\mathbb R$ and payoffs $\Phi_\ell:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb R$ (functions of the path), the fine level-$\ell$ approximation $P^f_\ell(z)=\Phi_\ell\big(\text{Euler–Maruyama path with step }T2^{-\ell}\text{ driven by }z\big)$.

**`emCoarse`**. The coarse level-$\ell$ approximation inside a level-$(\ell+1)$ sample: $P^c_\ell(z)=\Phi_\ell\big(k\mapsto S^c_{2k}\big)$, where $S^c$ is the coarse path with step $T2^{-(\ell+1)}$ driven by $z$.

**Formalization Note** Times are $t_i=ih$ with the index cast to $\mathbb R$. Payoffs are arbitrary functions of the path sequence; their measurability and integrability are hypotheses of the theorems that need them.
MLMC_EulerMaruyama.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §2, eqs. (2), (4), (5); M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 29.

MLMC_Implementation.definition_title: Giles (2015), §3.4: the floored estimates of the MLMC driver and the least-squares line used to estimate the rates
MLMC_Implementation.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.4, the driver routine `mlmc.m` of the MLMC algorithm.

**`floorEst`**. The driver does not let the estimates of the means and variances of the level corrections drop too fast: "the estimated $V_\ell$ … is not allowed to decrease by more than factor ½ relative to this anticipated value"; the code sets `ml(l) = max(ml(l), 0.5*ml(l-1)/2^alpha)` and `Vl(l) = max(Vl(l), 0.5*Vl(l-1)/2^beta)` for `l = 3:L+1` (levels $\ell\ge2$). For a sequence $x:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ and a factor $r\in\mathbb R$ (in the code $r=\tfrac12 2^{-\alpha}$ or $\tfrac12 2^{-\beta}$),
$$
\hat x_0=x_0,\qquad \hat x_1=x_1,\qquad \hat x_{\ell+2}=\max\big(x_{\ell+2},\;r\,\hat x_{\ell+1}\big).
$$

**`lsSlope`**, **`lsIntercept`**. The rates $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are "estimated by linear regression". For a finite index set $s$ and points $(t_i,y_i)_{i\in s}$ with means $\bar t=|s|^{-1}\sum_{i\in s}t_i$ and $\bar y=|s|^{-1}\sum_{i\in s}y_i$,
$$
\mathrm{lsSlope}=\frac{\sum_{i\in s}(t_i-\bar t)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_{i\in s}(t_i-\bar t)^2},\qquad \mathrm{lsIntercept}=\bar y-\mathrm{lsSlope}\cdot\bar t .
$$

**Formalization Note** Division by zero is $0$ in Lean; the theorems about the least-squares line assume $\sum_{i\in s}(t_i-\bar t)^2\ne0$, i.e. that not all $t_i$ are equal.
MLMC_Implementation.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.4, pp. 23–26 of the author's version (the MATLAB driver `mlmc.m`).

MLMC_PoissonCoupling.definition_title: Giles (2015), §8: tau-leaping for a continuous-time Markov chain and the Anderson–Higham coupling of the fine and coarse Poisson increments
MLMC_PoissonCoupling.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 55: "the 'tau-leaping' method … gives the discrete equation $x_{n+1}=x_n+P(h\lambda(x_n))$, where $h$ is the timestep, $\lambda(x_n)$ is the reaction rate (or propensity function), and $P(t)$ represents a unit-rate Poisson random variable over time interval $[0,t]$. If this equation defines the fine path in the multilevel simulation, then the coarse path, with double the timestep, is given by $x^c_{n+2}=x^c_n+P(2h\lambda(x^c_n))$ for even timesteps $n$." 

Giles (2015), §8, p. 55: "the first step is to express the coarse path Poisson variate as the sum of two Poisson variates, $P(h\lambda(x^c_n))$ corresponding to the first and second fine path timesteps. For the first of the two fine timesteps, the coarse and fine path Poisson variates are coupled by defining two Poisson variates based on the minimum of the two reactions rates, and the absolute difference, $P_1=P\big(h\min(\lambda(x_n),\lambda(x^c_n))\big)$, $P_2=P\big(h|\lambda(x_n)-\lambda(x^c_n)|\big)$, and then using $P_1$ as the Poisson variate for the path with the smaller rate, and $P_1+P_2$ for the path with the larger rate." 

Throughout, $\lambda:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ is the rate (propensity) function, $h\ge0$ the time step, the state is a count $x\in\mathbb N$, and $\mathrm{Po}(r)$ is the Poisson distribution with mean $r\ge0$ on $\mathbb N$ (Mathlib's `poissonMeasure`).

**`couplePair`**. For rates $a,b\ge0$ and $(p_1,p_2)\in\mathbb N^2$, the pair of increments of the paths with rates $a$ and $b$:
$$
\mathrm{couplePair}(a,b)(p_1,p_2)=\big(p_1+[\,b<a\,]\,p_2,\;\;p_1+[\,a<b\,]\,p_2\big),
$$
where $[\cdot]$ is $1$ if the condition holds and $0$ otherwise. The path with the smaller rate gets $p_1$, the path with the larger rate gets $p_1+p_2$.

**`coupledIncr`**. The joint law of the coupled increments: the image of $\mathrm{Po}(\min(a,b))\otimes\mathrm{Po}(\max(a,b)-\min(a,b))$ under $\mathrm{couplePair}(a,b)$.

**`tauStep`**. One tau-leaping step from the state $x$: the law of $x+P$ with $P\sim\mathrm{Po}(h\lambda(x))$.

**`tauChain`**. The law of the tau-leaping chain after $n$ steps from $x_0$: $\delta_{x_0}$ for $n=0$, and the composition of the law after $n$ steps with `tauStep` for $n+1$.

**`coupledTwoStep`**. Two coupled fine steps from the pair $(x,y)$ of fine and coarse states: first the coupled increments $(i,j)$ with rates $h\lambda(x)$, $h\lambda(y)$; then, from $x+i$, the coupled increments $(i',j')$ with rates $h\lambda(x+i)$ and $h\lambda(y)$ (the coarse rate stays frozen at $\lambda(y)$ over the coarse step). The result is $(x+i+i',\,y+j+j')$.

**`coupledChain`**. The law of the coupled pair after $k$ pairs of fine steps from $(x_0,x_0)$: $\delta_{(x_0,x_0)}$ for $k=0$, and the composition with `coupledTwoStep` for $k+1$.

**Formalization Note** The laws are measures on $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$; "composition" is `Measure.bind`. Rates are nonnegative reals (`ℝ≥0`), so $|a-b|=\max(a,b)-\min(a,b)$.
MLMC_PoissonCoupling.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 of the author's version (after D. Anderson and D. Higham, Multi-level Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, 2012).

MLMC_FixedPointPath.definition_title: Haas–Giles (2025), Algorithm 1: one time step of the geometric Brownian motion path decomposed into elementary operations, and the resulting path
MLMC_FixedPointPath.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §4.1, p. 8, Algorithm 1 "Geometric Brownian Motion path calculation (decomposed in elementary operations to show the intermediary fixed-point variables)":
$h\leftarrow T/N$; $con1\leftarrow r\times h$; $con2\leftarrow\sqrt h\times\sigma$; generate (approximate) random normal increments $\tilde Z_i$ for $i=1,\dots,N$; for $i=1,\dots,N$: $mul1_i\leftarrow con2\times\tilde Z_i$, $sum1_i\leftarrow con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i\leftarrow S_i\times sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}\leftarrow S_i+mul2_i$. "This algorithm details how we decomposed the operations to compute each time step from (13)", where (13) is $\tilde S_{i+1}=\tilde S_i+a(\tilde S_i,t_i)h+b(\tilde S_i,t_i)\sqrt h\,\tilde Z_i$.

**`gbmStep`**. For $r,\sigma,h,S,Z\in\mathbb R$, one step of Algorithm 1 in exact arithmetic:
$$
con1=rh,\quad con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma,\quad mul1=con2\cdot Z,\quad sum1=con1+mul1,\quad mul2=S\cdot sum1,\qquad \mathrm{gbmStep}(r,\sigma,h,S,Z)=S+mul2 .
$$

**`gbmPath`**. For $r,\sigma,h,s_0\in\mathbb R$ and increments $Z:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, the path $S_0=s_0$, $S_{i+1}=\mathrm{gbmStep}(r,\sigma,h,S_i,Z_i)$.

**Formalization Note** $\sqrt h$ is `Real.sqrt` (zero for $h<0$). The increments are indexed from $0$.
MLMC_FixedPointPath.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §4.1, p. 8, Algorithm 1, and (13).

MLMC_ML2RComplexity.definition_title: Giles (2015), §2.3: the uniform bound on the ML2R weights and the number of levels of multilevel Richardson–Romberg extrapolation
MLMC_ML2RComplexity.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.3, p. 12: "Because the remaining error is $O(2^{-\alpha L^2})$, rather than the usual $O(2^{-\alpha L})$, it is possible to obtain the usual $O(\varepsilon)$ weak error with a value of $L$ which is the square root of the usual value. Hence, in the case $\beta=\gamma$ they prove that the overall cost is reduced to $O(\varepsilon^{-2}|\log\varepsilon|)$, while for $\beta<\gamma$ the cost is reduced much more to $O(\varepsilon^{-2}2^{(\gamma-\beta)\sqrt{|\log_2\varepsilon|/\alpha}})$." (The remaining error is in fact of order $2^{-\alpha L(L+1)/2}$, see `ml2r_bias`.)

**`ml2rWeightBound`**. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, with $r=2^{-\alpha}$ and $B=e^{r/(1-r)^2}$:
$$
\mathrm{ml2rWeightBound}(\alpha)=\frac{B^2}{1-r}=\frac{\exp\!\big(r/(1-r)^2\big)^2}{1-r}.
$$
For $\alpha>0$ it bounds $\sum_\ell|w_\ell|$ uniformly in $L$ (`sum_abs_ml2rWeight_le`).

**`ml2rLevel`**. For $\alpha,c_1,\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$, the number of levels
$$
\mathrm{ml2rLevel}(\alpha,c_1,\varepsilon)=\Big\lceil\sqrt{2\max\big(0,\log_2(2c_1/\varepsilon)\big)/\alpha}\;\Big\rceil ,
$$
the natural-number ceiling.

**Formalization Note** $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is `Real.sqrt` and $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ is `Nat.ceil`; $\log_2$ is `Real.logb 2`.
MLMC_ML2RComplexity.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.3, p. 12 (after V. Lemaire and G. Pagès, Multilevel Richardson–Romberg extrapolation, 2013).

MLMC_MarkovChain.definition_title: Giles (2015), §10.1: the Markov chain started in the past, the σ-algebras of its noises, and the example $X_{n+1}=X_n/2+\xi_n$
MLMC_MarkovChain.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §10.1, p. 61: "the Markov chain $\{X_n\}$ in a metric space with metric $d$ is defined by $X_0=x$, $X_{n+1}=\varphi_n(X_n)$, $n\ge0$, where $\{\varphi_n\}$ is a sequence of iid random functions. Furthermore, it is assumed that the $\varphi$'s are contracting on average in the sense that $\sup_{x\ne y}\mathbb E\big[(d(\varphi_n(x),\varphi_n(y))/d(x,y))^{2\gamma}\big]<1$ for some $\gamma\in(0,1)$ … $f$ is Hölder continuous with exponent $\gamma$, so that $|f(y)-f(x)|\le d(x,y)^\gamma$. … Glynn and Rhee (2014) circumvent this problem by making $N$ increase with level, starting a level $\ell$ simulation at $n=-N_\ell$ and terminating it at $n=0$ … the level $\ell$ and $\ell-1$ simulations share the same random $\varphi_n$ for $n\ge-N_{\ell-1}$. Because of the contraction property, the effect of the initial evolution of the level $\ell$ path for $n<-N_{\ell-1}$ decays exponentially. This gives a coupling with a multilevel correction variance which decays as $\ell$ increases." 

**`backIter`**. For $\varphi:\alpha\to E\to\alpha$, $n\in\mathbb N$, noises $e:\mathbb N\to E$ and $x\in\alpha$:
$$
\mathrm{backIter}(\varphi,0,e,x)=x,\qquad \mathrm{backIter}(\varphi,n+1,e,x)=\varphi\big(\mathrm{backIter}(\varphi,n,(e_{k+1})_k,x),\,e_0\big),
$$
that is $\varphi(\cdot,e_0)\circ\varphi(\cdot,e_1)\circ\dots\circ\varphi(\cdot,e_{n-1})$ applied to $x$: the value at time $0$ of the chain started at time $-n$ at $x$ whose step ending at time $-k$ applies $\varphi(\cdot,e_k)$. The level $\ell$ sample of Giles is $\mathrm{backIter}(\varphi,N_\ell,e,x_0)$.

**`noiseFrom`**. For $\xi:\mathbb N\to\Omega\to E$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\xi_m,\xi_{m+1},\dots$:
$$
\mathrm{noiseFrom}(\xi,m)=\bigvee_{i\ge m}\sigma(\xi_i).
$$

**`halfStep`**. For $x,e\in\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{halfStep}(x,e)=x/2+e$ (the example chain $X_{n+1}=\tfrac12X_n+\xi_n$).

**`fairCoin`**. The measure $\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1$ on $\mathbb R$, the law of $\xi_n$ in the example ($\mathbb P(\xi_n=0)=\mathbb P(\xi_n=1)=\tfrac12$).

**`uniform02`**. The measure $\tfrac12\,\lambda|_{(0,2]}$ on $\mathbb R$ ($\lambda$ Lebesgue measure), the uniform distribution on $[0,2]$.
MLMC_MarkovChain.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §10.1, p. 61 (after P.W. Glynn and C.-H. Rhee, Exact estimation for Markov chain equilibrium expectations, 2014).

MLMC_PDEExamples.definition_title: Giles (2015), §7.1: the explicit step of the heat-equation scheme, and the Euler–Maruyama and Milstein steps
MLMC_PDEExamples.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §7.1, p. 51 (a 1D parabolic SPDE): "An Euler-Maruyama time discretisation with timestep $k$, combined with a second order space discretisation with uniform grid spacing $h$, gives the discrete approximation $u^{n+1}_j=u^n_j+\frac{k}{h^2}(u^n_{j+1}-2u^n_j+u^n_{j-1})+10\,\Delta W_n$. The level $\ell$ approximation uses $h_\ell=2^{-(\ell+1)}$, $k_\ell=\frac14h_\ell^2$. Keeping $k_\ell/h_\ell^2=\frac14$ ensures the explicit numerical discretisation is stable on all levels. Since the number of grid points doubles on each level, and the number of timesteps increases by factor 4, the cost per sample increases by factor 8, giving $\gamma=3$. Because the stochastic forcing is additive, i.e. the volatility does not depend on $u(x,t)$, the Euler-Maruyama discretisation is actually equivalent to a Milstein discretisation … the solution error is $O(2^{-2\ell})$ and hence $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=4$. This leads to the optimal complexity of $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$." 

**`heatStep`**. For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, a grid function $u:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ and $j\in\mathbb Z$, the noise-free explicit step
$$
\mathrm{heatStep}(\lambda,u)_j=u_j+\lambda\,(u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}),\qquad\lambda=k/h^2 .
$$

**`emStep`**. For $a,b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $h,S,\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the Euler–Maruyama step $\mathrm{emStep}(a,b,h,S,\Delta W)=S+a(S)h+b(S)\Delta W$.

**`milsteinStep`**. The Milstein step of Giles (2015), §5.2, $\mathrm{milsteinStep}(a,b,h,S,\Delta W)=S+a(S)h+b(S)\Delta W+\tfrac12\,b(S)\,b'(S)\,(\Delta W^2-h)$, where $b'$ is the derivative of $b$.

**Formalization Note** $b'(S)$ is Mathlib's `deriv b S` (zero where $b$ is not differentiable).
MLMC_PDEExamples.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §7.1, pp. 49–51. The Milstein step: §5.2, p. 35.

MLMC_SDEExtras.definition_title: Giles (2015), §5: the Brownian-bridge interpolant, the antithetic swap of increments, the explicit mean-reverting step and the smoothed CDF
MLMC_SDEExtras.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.2, pp. 38–39: "For the fine path, the interpolant for timestep $[t_n,t_n+h]$ is $\hat S^f(t)=\hat S^f_n+\lambda(\hat S^f_{n+1}-\hat S^f_n)+b^f_n(W(t)-W_n-\lambda(W_{n+1}-W_n))$ where $\lambda=(t-t_n)/h$ … the interpolant for the time interval $[t_n,t_n+2h]$ is $\hat S^c(t)=\hat S^c_n+\lambda(\hat S^c_{n+2}-\hat S^c_n)+b^c_n(W(t)-W_n-\lambda(W_{n+2}-W_n))$ where $\lambda=(t-t_n)/(2h)$ … We can now evaluate this interpolant at time $t_n+h$, obtaining $\hat S^c(t_{n+1})=\frac12(\hat S^c_n+\hat S^c_{n+2})+\frac12b^c_n((W_{n+1}-W_n)-(W_{n+2}-W_{n+1}))$ using the Brownian increments … already generated for the fine path." 

Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "The estimator which is used is $Y_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_i\frac12(P_\ell(\omega_i)+P_\ell(\omega^a_i))-P_{\ell-1}(\omega_i)$. Here $\omega_i$ represents the driving Brownian path, and $\omega^a_i$ is an antithetic counterpart defined by a time-reversal of the Brownian path within each coarse timestep. This results in the Brownian increments for the antithetic fine path being swapped relative to the original path. Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs" 

Giles (2015), §5.6, pp. 43–44: "If the drift term has a characteristic time-scale of $\tau$, as in a mean-reverting drift $(\theta-S_t)/\tau$, then when using the explicit Euler-Maruyama discretisation the timestep $h_0$ on the coarsest level cannot be much larger than $\tau$ without encountering severe numerical stability problems." 

Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "Pointwise values of the CDF … correspond to expected values of an indicator function, $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases." 

**`bridgeInterp`**. For $S_0,S_1,b,W_0,W_1,W_t,\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{bridgeInterp}(S_0,S_1,b,W_0,W_1,W_t,\lambda)=S_0+\lambda(S_1-S_0)+b\,(W_t-W_0-\lambda(W_1-W_0))$.

**`pairSwap`**. For $i\in\mathbb N$, $\mathrm{pairSwap}(i)=i+1$ if $i$ is even and $i-1$ if $i$ is odd: the permutation $2k\leftrightarrow2k+1$.

**`swapIncrements`**. For $z:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{swapIncrements}(z)_i=z_{\mathrm{pairSwap}(i)}$: the two fine increments of each coarse timestep exchanged.

**`emMeanRevert`**. For $\theta,\tau,h,S\in\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{emMeanRevert}(\theta,\tau,h,S)=S+\frac{\theta-S}{\tau}h$, the explicit Euler step for the drift $(\theta-S)/\tau$.

**`smoothCDF`**. For a measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$, $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $\delta,x\in\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{smoothCDF}(\mu,P,g,\delta,x)=\int_\Omega g\big((x-P(\omega))/\delta\big)\,d\mu(\omega)$.
MLMC_SDEExtras.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.2–§5.7, pp. 35–46.
